summary: India's traditional crafts include handloom weaving, block printing, embroidery, metal casting, pottery, woodwork, stone carving and folk painting, practised by hereditary craft communities in every state. Many have Geographical Indication (GI) tags, such as Banarasi sarees, Kanchipuram silk, Madhubani painting, Channapatna toys and Bidriware.

sections.h2: What counts as a traditional craft?
paras: A traditional craft is a skill for making useful or beautiful objects by hand, passed down within families or communities, usually over many generations. The object matters, but the heritage lies just as much in the knowledge: how to prepare a dye, judge a clay, set a loom or cast a bronze. That knowledge is a form of [intangible cultural heritage](what-is-intangible-cultural-heritage.html).

Archaeology shows how old some of these skills are. Harappan sites have produced cotton traces, carnelian beads drilled with fine borers, copper and bronze objects and wheel-thrown painted pottery. Our [pottery workshop](clay-and-the-past-a-pottery-workshop.html) uses that link between ancient and living practice.

sections.h2: Traditional crafts of India by type
list: Handloom weaving: silks of Banaras, Kanchipuram and Mysuru; Pochampally ikat; Chanderi and Maheshwari cottons; Muga silk of Assam.
Printing and dyeing: hand block printing at Bagru and Sanganer, Ajrakh in Kachchh, Kalamkari in Andhra Pradesh, bandhani tie-dye in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Embroidery: Chikankari of Lucknow, Phulkari of Punjab, Kantha of Bengal, Kasuti of Karnataka.
Metalwork: Bidriware of Bidar, Thathera brass and copper of Jandiala Guru, dhokra lost-wax casting in central and eastern India, bronze casting at Swamimalai.
Clay and terracotta: blue pottery of Jaipur, Khurja ceramics, terracotta horses of Bankura, Molela clay plaques in Rajasthan.
Wood and lacquer: Channapatna lacquered toys, Etikoppaka toys, Kashmiri walnut carving, Saharanpur wood carving.
Painting: Madhubani (Mithila), Pattachitra of Odisha, Warli of Maharashtra, Gond painting, Tanjore painting, Kalighat painting.
Stone: marble inlay (pietra dura) of Agra, stone carving of Mamallapuram.

sections.h2: GI tags: protecting crafts by place
paras: A Geographical Indication (GI) tag protects a product whose quality or reputation comes from a particular place. India's Geographical Indications of Goods Act came into force in 2003, and crafts form a large share of the registered GIs. A GI stops others from selling an imitation under the protected name, though enforcement is a continuing challenge.

paras: Most crafts were, and often still are, practised by hereditary communities: weaver groups, potters, metal casters, carpenters and painters, each with their own tools, terms and family workshops. Many craft towns grew around patrons such as temples, courts and trade routes. Moradabad brass, Saharanpur woodwork and Bidar's Bidriware all reflect that history.

Today craftspeople face competition from machine-made copies, rising costs of raw materials and young people moving to other jobs. Design schools, cooperatives, state emporia and fair-trade buyers have helped some crafts adapt. Seeing objects in a good collection, such as at the [National Crafts Museum in Delhi](national-crafts-museum-living-traditions.html), is the best way to understand the range.

Crafts also leave a trail for historians. Textiles from Gujarat have been found at Fustat in Egypt, and Indian beads and cloth travelled across the Indian Ocean for centuries. Museum labels, trade records and the objects themselves let researchers trace how designs moved between regions and how patrons shaped what was made.

list: Buy from the maker, a cooperative or a recognised state emporium when you can.
Ask how it was made: handloom and power loom, hand block and screen print look similar at a glance.
Look for the GI mark or the Handloom Mark on textiles.
Expect to pay more for real handwork; the price reflects days of labour.
Never buy antiquities or temple objects; their export and trade are regulated by law.

sections.h2: Traditional crafts of India: notes for students
list: Main groups: textiles, embroidery, metalwork, pottery, woodwork, painting, stone.
GI law: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, in force from 2003.
Examples with GI: Banarasi sarees, Kanchipuram silk, Madhubani painting, Channapatna toys, Bidriware, Pochampally ikat.
Lost-wax metal casting: dhokra (tribal communities of central and eastern India) and Swamimalai bronzes (Tamil Nadu).
Thathera metalwork of Jandiala Guru, Punjab, is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

faq.q: What are the traditional crafts of India?
faq.a: They include handloom weaving, block printing, tie-dye, embroidery, metal casting and inlay, pottery and terracotta, wood carving and lacquer work, folk and court painting, and stone carving and inlay. Each region has its own specialities, often linked to particular communities.

faq.q: Which Indian crafts have a GI tag?
faq.a: Many do. Well-known examples are Banarasi sarees and brocades, Kanchipuram silk, Pochampally ikat, Madhubani painting, Channapatna toys, Bidriware, Lucknow Chikan craft, Phulkari, Jaipur blue pottery, Pattachitra, Kashmir Pashmina and Muga silk of Assam.

Dhokra is metal casting by the lost-wax method, practised by tribal and artisan communities in states such as Chhattisgarh, Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand. A wax model is coated in clay, heated so the wax runs out, and molten brass is poured into the hollow.

faq.q: Which state is famous for which craft?
faq.a: Some pairs: Bihar for Madhubani painting, Karnataka for Channapatna toys and Bidriware, Uttar Pradesh for Banarasi silk and Chikankari, Odisha for Pattachitra, Gujarat for Ajrakh and bandhani, Rajasthan for block printing and blue pottery, and Assam for Muga silk.

posts.hook: Bidriware is black for a reason.
posts.caption: Craftsmen in Bidar blacken a zinc alloy with a special soil paste, so the silver inlay shines against it. The craft holds a GI tag.
